tldr: To run LLMs directly on robots with limited compute, the authors propose "BT-Agent," a Behavior Tree-based architecture that decouples reasoning from execution, achieving fully onboard operation with a 9B model and a highly efficient text and simulation evaluation pipeline.
hero_caption: A physical robot experiment running a 9B model fully onboard a Spot quadruped equipped with a Jetson Thor. Across five task categories including long-range navigation, landmark search, and physical panel manipulation, the agent succeeded in 11 out of 15 trials.
overview:
Using Large Language Models (LLMs) as the brains of robots is an exciting area of research, but relying solely on onboard compute without cloud resources suddenly raises the bar. Under severe memory and compute constraints, the robot must handle complex task reasoning while quickly reacting to unexpected obstacles or lost localization to stop and recover. Waiting for the model's next token output, as conventional setups do, cannot prevent dangerous collisions in time.

To address this, the authors developed "BT-Agent," which combines LLM-driven task-level decision-making with responsive execution control using Behavior Trees (BTs), a standard tool in robotics. The LLM simply selects and executes predefined BT skills, while precondition checks and safety monitoring (guards) inside each skill are handled autonomously by the BT on every tick. This allows the system to abort ongoing actions immediately without waiting for LLM re-inference, returning structured failure causes as feedback to the model.

There is also an innovation in evaluation. Because testing on physical robots and physics simulators is extremely expensive, the authors built a multi-fidelity benchmark combining a 161-task text environment and a 39-task physics simulation (Habitat) sharing identical task definitions and API contracts. The text environment runs 10.9× faster than simulation, enabling efficient verification of model robustness via controlled fault injection tests.

Experimental results show that BT-Agent improves task success rates by up to around 10 percentage points over strong Act/ReAct baselines, especially on smaller models (4B and 9B). Furthermore, physical experiments deploying a 9B model on a Spot quadruped confirmed fully onboard task completion and rapid intervention stops within 19 milliseconds.
contributions: Proposed "BT-Agent," an onboard robot architecture that decouples LLM task reasoning (ReAct loop) from responsive control via predefined Behavior Tree (BT) skills.

Constructed a 161-task multi-fidelity evaluation benchmark linking a text environment that evaluates at 10.9× the throughput of simulation with the Habitat physics simulator under shared task goals and skill contracts.
Conducted extensive comparisons across model sizes from 4B to 122B, revealing that smaller models benefit the most from structured tool calls and informative failure feedback.
Demonstrated fully onboard reasoning and control on a quadruped robot (Spot) using a 9B model, achieving a median 19 ms stopping response upon external interventions.

sections.heading: Why is running LLMs directly onboard robots so difficult?
sections.summary: Enabling autonomous mobile robots to follow high-level instructions requires balancing task reasoning with responsive physical execution under constrained onboard compute. This paper introduces "BT-Agent," blending flexible model reasoning with robust execution monitoring via Behavior Trees (BTs), supported by an evaluation pipeline combining fast text and high-fidelity simulation.
sections.details:
Recent research has actively explored issuing high-level natural language instructions to mobile robots. During exploration, inspection, and manipulation, robots must track partial observations and adapt flexibly whenever actions fail. To operate independently without relying on powerful external cloud servers, all this reasoning must run directly on the robot's onboard computer. However, onboard environments face tight resource constraints, competing for memory and compute with perception and low-level control processes.

Existing LLM-based agent systems excel at reasoning about what to do next through skill selection or code generation. Yet they lack a shared execution interface that defines how physical skills expose execution state, verify conditions, and rapidly abort during critical situations. Waiting for model inference is simply too slow for rapidly changing physical environments.

To solve this, the researchers turned to Behavior Trees (BTs), a proven control architecture in robotics. BT-Agent couples an "LLM Actor" that handles task-level decisions with predefined "BT skills." Guard conditions inside the BT skills monitor system state on every tick (periodic update), interrupting execution immediately upon anomalies without consulting the model. Furthermore, to evaluate this architecture efficiently, the authors developed a 161-task multi-fidelity benchmark and validated the system all the way to onboard physical robot experiments.

sections.heading: At the intersection of Behavior Trees and agent research
sections.summary: While previous works have used BTs for robot execution or applied LLM agents to physical hardware, evaluations under strict onboard compute limits have been scarce. Additionally, the multi-fidelity evaluation bridging text and simulation under identical goals and skill contracts provides a distinct advantage.
sections.details:
To understand where this work stands, consider three related areas of research:

- Behavior Trees (BTs) in robot execution: BTs offer modular and reactive control structures. Prior work includes PA-BT, which expands trees during execution, approaches using VLMs to generate trees with condition nodes, and BTGenBot-2, which generates and repairs executable trees using smaller models. However, many of these entrust tree generation itself to the model, raising safety verification challenges. Instead of letting the model build trees, BT-Agent has the LLM invoke human-verified, fixed BT skills.

- Agent systems and onboard deployment: Numerous studies show LLMs calling tools or generating code (such as Thea or RoboHarness), but most assume offboard compute. While pioneering examples deploy distilled planners or small VLMs directly onboard, systematic evaluations of task-level reasoning and execution safety under tight onboard constraints remain rare.

- Multi-fidelity evaluation: Efforts like BEHAVIOR-1K and ALFWorld bridge textual representations and physics simulations. BT-Agent's evaluation framework builds on this idea, fully unifying task goals and skill interfaces between text and a physics simulator (Habitat), while supporting controlled fault injection on the text side.

sections.heading: Decoupling the brain (LLM) from the reflexes (BT)
sections.summary: BT-Agent cleanly separates the LLM Actor, which performs high-level reasoning, from BT skills that carry fixed safety logic. The Actor selects skills in a ReAct loop, while the BT handles precondition checks and runtime guard evaluation autonomously, returning detailed diagnostic feedback on failures.
sections.details:
LLMs can propose inappropriate actions. For that reason, execution conditions must be enforced by the system rather than relying on model outputs. The core idea of BT-Agent is the clean separation between task-level selection and physical execution.

### III-A Agent (LLM Actor and reasoning loop)
The LLM Actor operates within a ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) framework. Based on the current task, past history, and stored data, it reasons about which skill to call next and determines its arguments. A higher-level supervisor BT activates skills one by one, returning the execution result and status to the Actor before the next reasoning step. The Actor receives summarized histories to conserve context length, and past outputs are stored in a typed object store. If a task cancellation is signaled, the ongoing skill can be aborted immediately.

### III-B BT Skills (defense via preconditions and guards)
Each robot skill (such as navigation or capturing an image) is implemented as a predefined Behavior Tree and exposed as a named tool. Developers can unit-test this execution logic ahead of time without worrying about model unpredictability.

Before a physical skill starts running, "Preconditions" are always verified. In navigation, for instance, the call is rejected right away if the target coordinates are unknown. During execution, "Guards" re-check conditions on every tick (the periodic BT update). If localization is lost or a timeout occurs during motion, the guard fails and sends an immediate stop request to the physical controller. This abort logic involves zero LLM inference, securing safety within milliseconds. When an action fails, structured diagnostic feedback detailing which guard or leaf failed is sent back to the Actor, allowing it to inspect the failure and try another approach.

sections.heading: Bridging fast text and realistic simulation for evaluation
sections.summary: Because iterative testing in physics simulators is computationally heavy, the authors built text and physical environments (Habitat/Isaac) sharing identical task definitions and skill interfaces. The text environment delivers over 10× higher throughput while enabling rigorous fault tolerance testing through injection.
sections.details:
Evaluating robot agents requires testing not only the model's reasoning capabilities but also how it recovers when perception or motion fails. However, running physics simulations every time is far too slow. This framework therefore provides multi-fidelity environments built from the same underlying scenes.

### IV-A Scene construction and task suite
The environments cover four scenes in total: two indoor scenes in Habitat, one outdoor scene in Isaac, and an additional indoor HSSD scene. The suite comprises 161 tasks in total: 50 primary tasks designed by human evaluators covering exploration, inspection, and manipulation, plus 111 transfer tasks to evaluate generalization to unseen environments.

### IV-B Unified execution substrate
From simulator geometry and camera captures, the authors pre-build a "scene memory" (object positions and descriptions), a navigation graph, and observable viewpoints. Text execution uses these records to rapidly update robot location and visibility states. Meanwhile, the Habitat physics simulation runs full VLM perception and local path planners, naturally introducing missed detections, false recognitions, and navigation snags.

### IV-C Task design and evaluation criteria
Tasks go beyond simple object finding to include egocentric captures, reading numbers or text for inspection, and physical push manipulation. All tasks are verified to be solvable via oracle action sequences, which also serve to establish step budgets.

### IV-D Fault injection
Evaluating only nominal success rates fails to reveal true robustness. The text environment injects controlled failures according to predefined rules—such as navigation timeouts, observation dropouts, or adversarial faults where an unfinished skill falsely reports success—testing whether the agent properly verifies outcomes and recovers.

sections.heading: Experimental results: onboard model performance, sim gaps, and real-world robots
sections.summary: Evaluated across the Qwen3.5 family (4B to 122B), BT-Agent outperformed existing baselines by up to 10 percentage points on smaller models (4B/9B). The text environment evaluated 10.9× faster than Habitat, and real-world Spot tests with a 9B model demonstrated fully onboard task success and rapid 19 ms stopping.
sections.details:
The experiments address three core questions (Q1: harness design on small models, Q2: bridging text and simulation evaluations, and Q3: responsive execution on physical hardware).

### V-B Model scale and harness design (Q1)
The authors compared BT-Agent against Act, ReAct, and Adapted CaP-X (code generation). Across all 161 tasks, BT-Agent matched or exceeded the ReAct baseline across all model sizes, with notable gains of 10.1 percentage points on 4B and 5.0 percentage points on 9B.
Ablation studies revealed that replacing structured tool calls (JSON) with natural language commands caused success rates to plummet, inflating token counts by 1.9× on 4B and 1.7× on 9B. Furthermore, simplifying failure feedback degraded success by 2 to 6 percentage points, showing that rich diagnostic information from the BT is critical for recovery in smaller models. BT-Agent also retained top performance under fault injection.
In Robosuite manipulation tasks, while code generation (CaP-X) excelled at long, regular sequences like raster scanning, BT-Agent's step-by-step decision-making achieved substantially higher success on tasks requiring reactive adjustments, such as re-stacking blocks based on observations.

### V-C From text evaluation to simulation (Q2)
Comparing 39 tasks in Habitat revealed a strong correlation between text and Habitat success rates (Spearman's $\rho = 0.61$). However, only 57.3% of the trials that succeeded in text also succeeded in Habitat. This highlights how real-world perception and locomotion failures heavily dictate physical outcomes even when symbolic reasoning succeeds.
In terms of throughput, with 8 parallel workers, the text environment processed 950 episodes per hour—10.9× faster than Habitat (87.3 episodes/hour). This validates a two-stage evaluation approach: rapidly screening designs in text and uncovering hidden pitfalls in simulation.

### V-D Real-world onboard operation and responsive execution (Q3)
The authors ran fully onboard experiments using a 9B model on a Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson Thor. Across five real-world tasks (long-range capture, landmark search, safe manipulation, etc.), the robot completed 11 out of 15 trials.
Furthermore, in intervention tests where external interruptions or timeouts were injected during navigation, the median latency from guard detection to zero robot command velocity was just 19 milliseconds. Given that the LLM's next inference step took 3.2 to 3.9 seconds, local BT guards are clearly essential for safe stopping.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: BT-Agent effectively combines high-level LLM reasoning with low-level Behavior Tree responsiveness, achieving autonomous robot execution under onboard compute constraints. Alongside its multi-fidelity evaluation suite, it offers practical design guidelines for deploying future robot agents.
sections.details:
This paper presents BT-Agent, a practical architecture for deploying LLM agents onboard real robots. By enforcing a clear division of responsibility—delegating task decisions to the model while keeping physical constraint verification and safety stops within the Behavior Tree—smaller models can achieve strong task completion rates alongside millisecond-level reactive safety.

### Limitations and future work
Several challenges remain. In the current design, BT skill implementations and guard logic are statically defined by developers; the model cannot synthesize new skills at runtime. Sensing also poses challenges when visual cues are ambiguous or partially missing, requiring better mechanisms to convey reliable evidence to the agent.
Promising future directions include pipelining LLM reasoning in parallel with skill execution monitoring, enabling models to directly interpret BT failure structures for more advanced recovery strategies, and leveraging fast executable text environments for reinforcement learning to optimize task-level policies.

takeaways: Completely separating reasoning (LLM) from execution and safety monitoring (BT) enables safe emergency stopping in 19 ms without waiting for model re-inference.
Smaller onboard models (4B and 9B) are highly sensitive to prompt and harness design; structured tool calling and informative failure feedback substantially boost their success rates.
A text evaluation environment sharing task contracts runs over 10× faster than physics simulation, making it ideal for rapid development iterations and fault-tolerance testing.
Only about 60% of symbolic/textual task successes translate to success in physical simulation, making a staged multi-fidelity evaluation pipeline essential.
limitations: Available BT skills and guard condition logic are statically fixed in advance; the model cannot dynamically synthesize new skills during execution.
Performance relies heavily on small VLM perception accuracy, making it prone to failure on tasks requiring high-resolution or fine-grained visual reasoning, such as reading clock dials.
No matter how robust an agent is in the text environment, it cannot fully predict physical simulation or real-world issues such as localization drift and visual occlusions.
